title: Flow cytometry
source: Prof. Abeer Mohammed, Flow cytometry lecture notes

sections.html:
Original page 2

Definitions

–Flowcytometry: It is the detection of cellular antigens during their movement in a fluid stream.

○Flow: moving in a fluid stream.

○Cyto: cellular.

○Metry: measurement.

–Dot Plot: A two parameter data graph used for acquisition and analysis. Each dot on the display represents one event that the flow cytometer analyzed.

–Event: It is the unit of data representing one particle or cell.

–Threshold: Signals can be made by a variety of sources that are unrelated to experimental data; stray light, dust, very small particles, and debris.

Original page 3

Principle

Open the clean redrawn version of this figure in the app →

Original page 4

–Passing of single cells through a laser source.

–Measurement of the scattered and emitted fluorescence using detectors:

○Scattered light:

➢Size: Forward scatter parallel to the laser beam

➢Nuclear complexity and cytoplasmic granularity: Side scatter detected at a 90˚ angle to the laser beam.

○Emitted fluorescence:Protein expression: Fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies can tag individual cells to further delineate their antigenic profile.

–Data interpretation.The detected light signal is converted into a digital signal proportional to its light emission and is plotted on a histogram.

Original page 5

Basic Components

–The Flow Chamber (fluidics):

○Sheath fluid: Cells are injected (under high pressure) into the sheath fluid stream (of lower pressure but faster than the injected sample → hydrodynamic focusing

Original page 6

○Coincidental events: passing 2 or more cells through the laser simultaneously → only one event being recorded → loss of data.

–The Optical System:

Open the clean redrawn version of this figure in the app →

○The laser source: Emitting light

○Mirrors: Directing the emitted light to detectors

Original page 7

○Filters: Block certain wavelengths (by absorption) while transmitting others:

▪Long pass filters: Allow light above a cutoff wavelength

▪Short pass filters: Permit light below a cutoff wavelength

▪Band pass filters: Transmit light within a specified narrow range of wavelengths (termed a band width).

Original page 8

▪Dichroic filter: Placed at an angle to the oncoming light to pass specified wavelengths in the forward direction and deflect the blocked light at a 90° angle.

○Detectors: photodiodes and photomultiplier tubes.

–Electronics:

○The light signals (photons) hit one side of the PMT or the photodiode, and are converted into a proportional number of electrons.

○The pulse returns to the baseline as the particle leaves the laser beam.

○Then to convert the analog information to digital information that can be processed by the computer and software using Analog to Digital Converters (ADC’s) which in turn allows for events to be plotted on a graphical scale (Histograms) to detect :

▪Proportion of cells

▪Intensity of the fluorescence: The fluorescence intensity emitted is proportional to the quantity of binding sites for the fluorescent compound on the cell/particle. So the more binding sites there are, the more fluorescence is emitted, and therefore the higher on the fluorescence intensity scale the data appears.

–Computer - Data Analysis

Original page 9

Sample preparation

–Fresh samples are required. Dead and dying cells have:

○Reduced Ag expression

○Non-specific binding

○Increased background fluorescence

–Appropriate controls should always be carried out

–Staining: 7

○Adjust the cell suspension to a concentration of 1 x 10 cells/ml with cold (4°C) PBS.

○Selecting the correct concentration of an antibody: according to the manufacturer recommendation or through staining positive cells with the antibody at a series of concentrations, usually using 'doubling dilutions. Example, 1:50, 1:100, 1:200, etc (Titration) and incubating cells with similar concentrations of an isotype control

Original page 10

Interpretation

–Light scattered in the forward direction, typically up to 20° offset from the laser beam’s axis and collected by the photodiode. It equates roughly to the particle’s size.

–Light measured at an approximately 90° angle to the excitation line. It provides information about the relative complexity (for example, granularity and internal structures) of a cell or particle.

–Measurements taken at different wavelengths can provide quantitative and qualitative data about fluorophore-labeled cell surface receptors or intracellular molecules such as DNA and cytokines.

–Steps:

○Identifying the cells of interest and gating on them.

○Gating: The First step in gating is typically to distinguish the cells based on CD45 vs side scatter properties: (Flow differential). CD45 is expressed on all nucleated

Original page 11

hematopoietic cells and is used as a first line gating marker to exclude debris and non-hematopoietic cells:

▪Lymphocytes (Red) express low SS and bright CD45.

▪Granuolocytes (Blue) express high SS and bright CD45.

▪Monocytes (Violet) express moderate SS and bright CD45.

▪Blasts (Green) (if present) are dim to negative CD45 and variable SS.

▪Apoptotic cells, erythroid precursors and plasma cells are negative CD45 and variable SS.

Open the clean redrawn version of this figure in the app →

○Seqential gating: Gates can be combined with each other in a specific sequence. EX: Lymphocytes were gated in CD45 /side scatter plot.This gate was used to set a gate on CD2+/CD20- (T lymphocytes) cells on the CD2/CD20 plot.Both regions were used to determine the CD2+/CD8+ in the CD2 versus CD8 plot.

Original page 12

–Data can be analyzed as histograms or in two-parameter dot:

○A histogram is a single parameter plot where the x-axis represents the parameter’s signal value in channel numbers and the y-axis represents the number of events per channel number. Using statistical tools, it can calculate percentage of cells manifesting specific fluorescence, and fluorescence intensity.

▪Determination of the fluorescence of cells stained with the isotype control (non-specific binding). Negative staining is defined by fluorescent intensity similar to that of a negative control.

▪The mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of a population of cells is linearly related to the mean number of antigens/cell.

Original page 13

○Two parameter or bivariate:They display two measurement parameters, one on the x-axis and one on the y-axis. They are display as a density (dot) plot or contour map:

▪Density plot: Each dot or point represents an individual cell that has passed through the instrument.The color intensity plots are the most common way to represent a density plot.

▪Contour diagram: The graph takes on the appearance of a geographical survey map. Each contour line representing a change in elevation (in number of events).

•Positivity of markers: The threshold of 20% should be used to define a positivity, except for MPO, CD79a, CD34, and TdT, which are considered positive at the 10% level of expression.

Panels

–Lineage markers.

–Markers of clonality.

–Markers of the stage of maturation.

–Markers for more specifications.

Original page 14

•Hematological Malignancies: These are group of disease characterized by clonal uncontrolled growth of hematopoietic cells.

•Diagnosis of hematological malignancies needs a combination of clinical findings, morphology, cytochemistry, immunophenotyping, and genetic tests.

Immunophenotypic Characteristics of Malignant Hematological Cells

–Clonality.

–Aberrant antigen expression.

–Disproportionate increase of one cell population.

Value of Flowcytometry in Diagnosis of Hematological Malignancies

–Confirmation of Clonality:

▪Monoclonal phenotyping

▪Light chain restriction in B lymphocyte neoplasms

–Determination of the lineage:

toc: Role of Flowcytometry in Diagnosis of Acute Leukemia
General flowyctometric characters of malignant cells in acute leukemia
sections.html:
Original page 17

•Acute leukemia: It a heterogeneous aggressive malignant disorder of hematopoietic cells, in which malignant transformation occurs in the hematopoietic stem cell or early progenitors resulting in clonal expansion of blasts in the bone marrow, peripheral blood, or other tissues with arrest of differentiation leading to accumulation of blasts and suppression of hematopoiesis.

2016 WHO Classification of Acute leukemia

–Acute Myeloid Leukemia

–Precursor Lymphoid Neoplasms

Role of Flowcytometry in Diagnosis of Acute Leukemia

–Confirmation of diagnosis: Confirmation of presence of blasts (Malignant cells in acute leukemia).

–It may help enumeration of blasts in the peripheral blood but not in bone marrow:

○Blasts in peripheral blood and especially Bone marrow blasts are better evaluated by morphology and not by flowcytometry

○Flowcytometry is not preferred for blast enumeration in bone marrow:

▪Sampling is labile to hemodilution.

▪Variable lysis of erythroid precursors.

–Lineage determination:

○The most valuable markers to differentiate blast types:

▪AML: CD13/CD33/CD117

▪B-ALL: CD10/CD19/cytoplasmic CD79a

▪T-ALL: cytoplasmic CD3

Original page 18

○Acute leukemia (CD34 +/– , TdT +/– , HLA-DR +/– , CD38 +/– ) without any specific myeloid or lymphoid markers, including cCD3, MPO, cCD22, cCD79a, and strong CD19, is classified as acute undifferentiated leukemia

–Determination of leukemia specific phenotype which is very important in detection of MRD.

General flowyctometric characters of malignant cells in acute leukemia

–CD45/ Side scatter: Blasts (Green) are dim to negative CD45 and variable SS.

–Expression of markers of immaturity:

○Expression of markers of immaturity as TdT, CD34, and/or CD117. The CD45/CD34 dot plot may be useful to identify malignant cell in acute leukemia:

Original page 19

○However CD34 may be negative in many cases of acute leukemia.

○Myeloid blasts are CD117+ and CD34+.

○Blasts with less differentiation may be positive for TdT.

○Blasts lacking the expression of immaturity markers can be identified by being CD16-, CD10-, and/or CD56 bright

○Benign maturing myeloid cells are CD16+, CD10+, and CD56–.

–Lack of expression of markers of maturity: Lack of expression of markers of maturity as CD10, CD11b, CD15, CD16, or CD65.

–HLA-DR:

○AML: positive in most cases, except for APL B-ALL : positive

○T-ALL: expressed only in few cases

–Leukemia-Associated Phenotype: This is the aberrant immunophenotype displayed by neoplastic cells which helps to differentiate minimal residual disease from normal marrow precursors:

○Abnormal intensity.

○Asynchronus expression of both markers of maturity and markers of immaturity.

○Homogeneous expression of an antigen usually expressed at varying levels during blast maturation.

○Expression of antigens of other lineages.

○Blasts may be aberrantly CD2+: acute monoblastic leukemia, hypogranular APL or AML with/without maturation

○Blasts may be CD7 dim/moderate, CD19+, CD56+ or Coexpress CD19 and CD56 “t(8;21)”.

Original page 20

Monoclonal Antibody Panel

–CD45 (pan-leucocyte marker) help to distinguish nonhemopoietic cells.

–Progenitor cells: CD34, CD117 and HLA-DR. CD34, or TdT are helpful to differentiate acute leukemia from leukemic phase of large cell lymphoma.

–Myeloid lineage: CD13, CD33 CD15 and MPO

–Monocytic lineage: CD33, CD14, CD64 and CD36

–Erythroid lineage: CD235a (glycophorin a) and CD71

–Megakaryocytic lineage: CD41, and CD61

–B-lymphoid lineage: CD19, CD79a and CD10

–T-lymphocyte lineage: CD3 1-Initial McAb panel: Distinguish AML from ALL and classify ALL into B- or T:

○B-lymphoid markers: CD19, CD10, cytoplasmic CD22 and cyt CD79a

○T- lymphoid markers: CD2,CD7 and cytoplasmic CD3

○Myeloid markers: CD13, CD33, CD117, cytoplasmic MPO

○Nonlineage specific markers: expressed in hemopoietic progenitor cells: CD 34, HLA-DR and TdT. 2-Second panel: Further classification:

○B-lymphoid markers: Cy mμ, sIg

○T- lymphoid markers: CD1a, CD5, CD4, CD8, anti-TCR

○Myeloid markers: CD41,CD42, CD61, antiglycophorin A

•2016 WHO Classification of AML:The diagnosis of the WHO categories of AML requires the careful integration of clinical history, morphology, and cytogenetic/molecular genetic analysis, supplemented by immunophenotyping in the residual category of AML, not otherwise specified:

–AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities

–AML with myelodysplasia-related changes

Original page 21

–Therapy-related myeloid neoplasms

–Acute myeloid leukemia, NOS

–Myeloid sarcoma

–Myeloid proliferations associated with Down syndrome

AML with t(8;21 )(q22;q22.1 ); RUNX1-RUNX1T1:

•This genetic abnormality is enough to diagnose AML even if Blasts are less than 20%.

•Corresponding FAB category: M2 Eos or M2 Baso.

•Morphology: It shows differentiation to mature neutrophils which may be dysplastic. Sometimes there is eosinophilic differentiation. Blast cells have an indentation in the nucleus, representing the Golgi zone, and often there is a long thin or fusiform Auer rod sometime within the nuclear “hof”.

•Cytochemistry: Blasts are positive for MPO, SBB and specific esterase. Blasts are negative for non-specific esterase and acid phosphatase.

•Immunophenotyping:

–Blasts are dim to negative CD45 and variable SS.

Open the clean redrawn version of this figure in the app →

Original page 22

–Expression of markers of immaturity: CD34 and CD117.

–Expression of myeloid markers: cyt MPO, CD13 and CD33

–Expression of markers of maturity : CD15 and/or CD65 but not CD11b.

Original page 23

–Aberrant weak expression of the B-lineage antigen, CD19

–Expression of CD56 “poorer prognosis”.

ML with inv(16)(p13.1;q22) or t(16;16)(p1 3.1;q22); CBFB-MYH11 :

•Corresponding FAB category: M4 Eos.

•Morphology:Acute myelomonocytic leukemia with eosinophilia. Bone marrow shows an increase in eosinophils and their precursors which contain large proeosinophilic granules even when the number of eosinophils is low.

•Cytochemistry: Myeloblasts are positive for specific esterase, MPO and SBB. Monoblasts and promonocytes are positive for non-specific esterase although it may be weaker than expected or even absent in some cases. Eosinophils are aberrantly positive for the specific esterase with faint positivity.

•Immunophenotyping: Multiple blast populations:

–CD45/side scatter: Myeloblasts have Low SSC /CD45 moderate while monoblasts have High SSC/CD45 moderate

–Markers of immaturity: Blasts show strong positive expression of CD34 and CD117.

Original page 24

–Myeloid markers: A subpopulation of blasts is positive for CD33, CD13 and MPO.

–Markers of maturation: A subpopulation of cells is positive for CD15 and CD65. Maturation asynchrony is often seen.

Myeloblasts Lympocytes Granulocytes Monoblast

–Monocytic markers: A subpopulation of blasts is positive for CD14, CD4, CD11b, CD11c, CD64 CD36, and lysozyme.

Original page 25

–Aberrant markers: Blasts are positive for CD2.

Myeloblasts Lympocytes Granulocytes Monoblast

–Negative markers of other lineages

Acute promyelocytic leukemia with PML-RARA:

•Corresponding FAB category: M3 and M3 variant.

•Morphology: Irregular and greatly variable nuclear size and shape. Nuclei are often kidney- shaped or bilobed. The cytoplasm is filled by densely packed large granules, bright pink, red, or purple. Granules may be so large and/or numerous that they totally obscure the nuclear- cytoplasmic margin. Auer rods are usually larger than those in other types of AML. Bundles of Auer rods “faggots” randomly distributed within the cytoplasm

Original page 26

Abnormal promyelocytes in the variant type are characterized by: An apparent paucity or absence of granules which may cause confusion with acute monocytic leukemia. The hypogranular appearance of the cytoplasm is due to the submicroscopic size of the azurophilic granules. Bilobed nuclei.

Immunophenotyping

–CD45/SS: CD45 brighter/Slightly increased SSC

–Markers of immaturity: CD117+, HLA-DR- and CD34-. CD34 may be + in microgranular variant.

Original page 27

–Myeloid markers: Homogeneous bright expression of CD33 and heterogeneous expression of CD13.

–Aberrant markers: CD2 may be positive in microgranular variant. CD56 is expressed in approximately 10% of cases and is associated with bad prognosis.

AML with t(9; 11 )(p21.3;q23.3); KMT2A-MLL T3 :

•Corresponding FAB category: M5a and occasionally M2 or M1.

•Morphology: Cytological features are usually those of acute monoblastic leukemia but sometimes of acute monocytic or acute myelomonocytic leukemia. There are no specific cytological clues to this diagnosis.

•Cytochemistry: Monoblasts and promonocytes are usually strongly positive for non- specific esterase. Monoblasts and promonocytes are negative for MPO.

Immunophenotyping

–CD45/ side scatter: Monoblasts have High SSC/CD45 moderate

Original page 28

–Markers of immaturity: Strong expression of HLA DR and weak expression of CD34 and CD117.

–Myeloid markers: Strong expression of CD33, weak expression of CD13 and negative expression of MPO.

–Markers of maturity: Strong expression of CD65.

Original page 29

–Monocytic markers: Positive expression of CD11b, CD11c, CD64, CD36, and CD36, variable expression of lysozyme, strong expression of CD4 and weak expression of CD14.

–Aberrant markers: Expression of CD56.

–Negative markers of other lineages

Original page 30

AML with t(6;9)(p23;q34.1 ); DEK-NUP2 14:

•Corresponding FAB category: It may correspond to any FAB category of AML except for M3 and M7; most commonly M2 or M4.

•Morphology: There are often dysplastic features. Sometimes there is basophilic differentiation with both peripheral blood and bone marrow basophils can be increased. Some patients also have an increase in bone marrow eosinophils.

Immunophenotyping

–Markers of immaturity: Blasts are positive for HLA DR, CD117 and CD34.

–Myeloid markers: Blasts are positive for MPO, CD13 and CD33.

–Basophil markers: Basophils are positive for CD123, CD33 and CD38.

–Monocytic markers: Blasts are positive for CD64.

Original page 31

AML with inv(3)(q21.3;q26.2) or t(3;3)(q21.3;q26.2); GATA2, MECOM:

•Corresponding FAB category: Mostly M2, M4 and M7.

•Morphology: Dysplastic megakaryocytes. Normal or even an increased platelet count. Differentiation can be granulocytic, myelomonocytic, or monoblastic/monocytic, but megakaryocytic differentiation is over-represented. Trilineage myelodysplasia can be present.

Immunophenotyping

–Markers of immaturity: Blasts are positive for CD34, CD117 and HLA-DR. CD34 expression is stronger with inv(3) than with t(3;3).

–Myeloid markers: Blasts are positive for CD33 and CD13.

–Basophil markers: Basophils are positive for CD38.

–Megakaryocytic markers: Some cases are positive for CD41 and CD61.

–Aberrant markers: Blasts are positive for CD7.

AML (megakaryoblastic) with t(1;22)(p13.3;q13.1); RBM15-MKL1:

•Corresponding FAB category: M7.

•Morphology: This subtype of AML typically occurs in infants and this, combined with the cytological features (basophilic blast cells with cytoplasmic blebs), can lead to a strong suspicion of the diagnosis

Original page 32

Immunophenotyping

–Megakaryocytic markers: CD41, CD61, and CD42b.

–Myeloid markers: Negative MPO but CD13 and CD33 may be positive.

–Markers of immaturity: negativeCD34, and HLA-DR

–CD45 is often negative.

–CD36 is characteristically positive.

–Lymphoid markers: Negative.

Original page 33

AML with BCR-ABL 1:

•No specific cytological features.

•Immunophenotyping: Myeloid antigens with Aberrant expression of CD7 and CD19

AML with mutated NPM1:

•Morphology: Blasts with cup-shaped nuclei, either:

–Acute myeloblastic leukemia with or without maturation

–Acute myelomonocytic or monocytic/monoblastic leukemia

Immunophenotyping

–Positive CD33, CD117, and MPO in cases with myeloblastic differentiation.

–Cases with monocytic differentiation: Positive CD64, CD14, and/or CD11b.

–CD34 is negative in 2/3 of cases

–HLA-DR is negative in 1/3 of cases “APL-like”

–CD4 or CD19 may be positive

Original page 34

AML with biallelic mutation of CEBPA :

•Corresponding FAB category: M2 or M1 but some cases correspond to M4 or M5.

•Morphology: There are no cytological clues to this diagnosis, except for the frequent association with erythroid dysplasia.

•Immunophenotyping: Cases with biallelic mutation of CEBPA have a higher frequency of HLA-DR, CD7, and CD15 expression and a lower frequency of CD56 expression than cases with a single mutation.

Provisional entity: AML with mutated RUNX1:

•Morphology: Corresponds to any FAB category especially M0. Other cases corresponds to M1, M4 or M5. It is associated with lower hemoglobin, lower white blood cell and lower peripheral blood blast cell counts than AML cases with the wild type RUNX1.

•Immunophenotyping: Aberrant expression of CD56 or CD7.

AML cases associated with

–Multtilineage dysplasia

–Prior history of a MDS syndrome or MDS/MPN

–MDS-related cytogenetic abnormalities

After exclusion of

–AML-related translocation, inversion or BCR-ABL1, somatic NPM1 mutations and somatic biallelic CEBPA mutations

–Therapy related AML cases

Original page 35

•Immunophenotyping: Variable results:

–Abnormal patterns of antigen expression and abnormal light-scattering.

–Cases with prior MDS are associated with positive CD34.

–Myeloid markers: positive with an aberrant high or low expression.

–Strong CD14 expression is related to a poor prognosis.

–CD11b expression is associated with the high-risk karyotypes.

–CD34, TdT, and CD7 expression are associated with abnormalities of chromosomes 5 and 7.

–Aberrant markers: Blasts often express CD56 and/or CD7.

–Multilineage dysplasia is associated with decreased expression of HLA-DR, CD117, FLT3 (CD135) and CD38 and increased expression of lactoferrin.

Therapy-related myeloid neoplasms

•Diagnosis is dependent on the clinical history and morphology

•Multilineage dysplasia is common.

•Immunophenotyping: Variable results similar to the de novo counterparts:

–Blasts are CD34 positive.

–The maturing myeloid cells show abnormal patterns of antigen expression and abnormal light-scattering.

–Blasts express panmyeloid antigens such as CD13, CD33, and MPO, with downregulation of MPO in some patients.

sections.html:
Original page 36

•AML with minimal differentiation.

•AML without maturation.

•AML with maturation.

•Acute myelomonocytic leukemia.

•Acute monoblastic and monocytic leukemia.

•Pure erythroid leukemia: can be suspected from morphology, and confirmed by the positive CD235a (glycophorin A) and often also CD36 and strong CD71.

•Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia: can be suspected from morphology, and confirmed by the positive CD41, CD42, and/or CD61. However, t(1; 22) must be excluded.

•Acute basophilic leukemia: can be suspected morphologically and confirmed by the positive CD123, CD203c, and CD11b in addition to other myeloid antigens. CD22 may be expressed. HLA-DR is negative.

Original page 37

•Acute panmyelosis with myelofibrosis: Diagnosis of acute panmyelosis with myelofibrosis is dependent on bone marrow morphology, but specifically on biopsy rather than aspiration. Immunohistochemistry, shows multilineage involvement.

•Expression of a single, relatively non-specific myeloid-associated antigen as CD13 or CD33, on only some blasts with other markers of immaturity as CD34, and HLA-DR is typical of acute undifferentiated leukemia. TdT and CD7 may be aberrantly positive.

Myeloid sarcoma:

•Morphology and immunophenotyping are important in diagnosis.

•Morphology may be myeloblastic, myelomonocytic, or monoblastic/monocytic. Sometimes there is eosinophilic or neutrophilic differentiation.

•Immunohistochemistry is important for differentiating it from other tumor

Myeloid proliferations associated with Down syndrome:

•It occurs during the first 5 years of life, in children

Morphology

–Megakaryoblasts are characteristic and there can be prominent

–Megakaryocytic differentiation with the presence of giant and hypogranular platelets.

–Other lineages abnormalities with circulating erythroblasts and myeloblasts.

–Sometimes there is basophilic differentiation.

•Immunophenotyping and bone marrow examination are not needed.

Precursor Lymphoid Neoplasms

Original page 38

•Definition: They are clonal malignancies of precursor lymphoid cells committed to the B cells, T cells and natural killer cells lineage, involving bone marrow and peripheral blood (ALL) or lymph nodes and extranodal sites (lymphoblastic lymphomas).

2016 WHO classification of precursor lymphoid neoplasms

–B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, non-otherwise specified.

–B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with recurrent genetic abnormalities.

–T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.

–NK-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.

sections.html:
•Morphology: B-Lymphoblasts are relatively uniform in appearance and vary from small blasts with scant cytoplasm, condensed nuclear chromatin, and indistinct nucleoli to larger cells with moderate amounts of light-blue to bluish-grey cytoplasm which is occasionally vacuolated, dispersed nuclear chromatin, and multiple variably prominent nucleoli. Nuclei are round to oval, indented, or convoluted. Coarse azurophilic granules in 10% of cases. There may be cytoplasmic pseudopods (hand-mirror).

Original page 39

Immunophenotyping

–Most cases are low SSC /CD45dim but may be CD45 negative or moderate.

–B Lymphoblasts are TdT+, CD34+, HLA-DR+ and CD117-.

–Lymphoblasts are positive for a combination of B-cell markers CD19, cCD79a, and cCD22, either strong expression of CD19 with one of the other B lineage markers or weak expression of CD19 with two of the other B lineage markers.

Original page 40

–CD19 and cytoplasmic CD22 are the most sensitive marker of B-cell lineage.

–B-lymphoblasts are CD19+, CD22+, and CD79a+, CD20-, and CD10 bright.

Morphology

–T- Lymphoblasts may be a considerable size range, from small lymphoblasts with very condensed nuclear chromatin and no evident nucleoli to larger blasts with finely dispersed chromatin and relatively prominent nucleoli. They may ocasionally resemble more mature lymphocytes:

○Cytoplasm: Scanty with possibility of cytoplasmic vacuoles.

○Nuclei: Round, irregular or convoluted.

○N:C ratio: High.

•Cytochemistry: Focal acid phosphatase activity.

Immunophenotyping

–T-lymphoblasts have slightly increased forward scatter when compared to benign T-cells.

Blasts Lymphocytes

sections.html:
Original page 63

•Definition: They are clonal malignancies characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of mature T lymphoid cells.

•Epidemiology: This group account for 10–12% of all lymphoid malignancies.

Diagnosis

–Detailed clinical data.

–Flowcytometry

–Morphology

–T-cell clonality

–Cytogenetic/FISH

–Viral studies

–In many cases flowcytometry can only suspect a T-cell lymphoma as it can’t define T cell clonality.

–However, Flowcytometry is an important, integral part of lymphoma diagnosis even in cases where it cannot give a definitive diagnosis.

Benign T cells vs Malignant T cells

–Benign T-cells are positive for pan-T-cell markers (CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7), CD4 or CD8, CD43, CD45 and TCR α β , and negative for HLA-DR.

–An abnormal antigen is generally not a reliable sign for T-cell malignancy, especially if it only concerns a few cells.

–Unusual T-cell populations may appear in many reactive conditions.

–Defining clonality is difficult (molecular testing of TCR gene rearrangement)

–The CD4/CD8-Ratio of T-cells shows some similarity to the kappa/lambda ratio but not equivalent tool to detect monoclonality

–only extreme alterations of the CD4/CD8-Ratio may be regarded as indicator of T- cell monoclonality only if caused by an increase of a T-cell population.

Original page 64

Flowcytometric characteristics of mature T-cell neoplasms

–High forward scatter: as in anaplastic large cell lymphoma, large cell type of peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified, few cases of T-cell large granular lymphocyte leukemia and others.

–Abnormal expression for 3 or 4 of the pan-T markers: Dim expression for 3 or 4 of the pan-T markers (CD2, CD3, CD5, and/or CD7) OR Dim expression for one or two markers if accompanied by other abnormalities

○Complete loss of a marker is more specific than the dim expression

○Variable (“smeary”; heterogeneous) expression.

○Loss of CD7 is frequent.

○However, positive expression of all pan-T antigens does not exclude T-cell neoplasm and dim/- expression may occur in reactive cases.

Original page 65

–CD45:

○Loss of CD45 can’t occur in reactive disorders.

○It is rarely observed in mature T-cell neoplasms but is highly suspicious for malignancy as in T cell prolymphocytic leukemia and anaplastic large T cell lymphoma.

–TCR: Dim α β, positive γ δ or lack of both indicates malignancy.

CD4/CD8 Expression

–Normally, the CD4/CD8-T-Cell ratio in peripheral blood is about 2:1.

–Restriction, dual-positive or dual-negative raise the possibility of malignancy especially if accompanied by an increase of the T cell population, although this is not diagnostic as it may occur in reactive cases. It may be also masked by the residual benign T-cells.

–Dual positive or dual negative expression is more often seen in T-ALL, whereas CD4 expression is more typical for mature T cell neoplasms.

–Mature T cell neoplasms may be:

○CD4 + /CD8 – :

▪Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma

▪Sezary syndrome/mycosis fungoides

▪Most cases of T cell prolymphocytic leukemia

▪Most cases of peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified

▪Most cases of anaplastic large T cell lymphoma.

○CD4 - /CD8 +:

▪T cell large granular cell leukemia

▪Panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma

▪Enteropathy-associated T-cell leukemia

▪Few cases of peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified

▪Few cases of T cell prolymphocytic leukemia

Original page 66

▪Few cases of anaplastic large T cell lymphoma

▪Rare cases of hepatosplenic T-cell lymphomas.

○CD4 + /CD8 +:

▪Few cases of T cell prolymphocytic leukemia

▪Few cases of T cell large granular cell leukemia

▪Rare cases of of peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified

▪Rare cases of anaplastic large T cell lymphoma.

○CD4 - /CD8 – :

▪Enteropathy-associated T-cell leukemia

▪NK-cell large granular cell leukemia

▪Extranodal T/NK-cell lymphoma (nasal type)

▪Hepatosplenic γ δ T-cell lymphomas

▪Peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified

▪T cell prolymphocytic leukemia

▪T cell large granular cell leukemia.

NK-cell associated markers (CD16, CD56, and/or CD57)

–They are expressed in T cell large granular T cell leukemia and T/NK-cell neoplasms.

–CD56 may be expressed in peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified, anaplastic large T cell lymphoma, and hepatosplenic γ δ T-cell lymphoma. It may be dimly expressed in reactive conditions.

•Aberrant expression of the pan-myeloid markers, CD13, and/or CD33 is not seen in mature T-cell neoplasms.

•Expression of CD117 in T cell prolymphocytic leukemia.

•B-cell associated markers (CD19 and/or CD20) are expressed in some cases of peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified.

Original page 67

•CD30:It is expressed by anaplastic large T cell lymphoma, peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified, enteropathy-associated T-cell leukemia and angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma.

•CD10 expression as in few cases of peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified.

•CD103 is expressed in enteropathy-associated T-cell leukemia.

T-Cell Prolymphocytic Leukemia

•CD45+

•HLA-DR-, CD1a-, TdT-, and CD34-.

•CD3+, CD2+, CD5+, CD7+, TCRαβ+, and CD52+.

•CD4+/CD8-, CD4-/CD8+ “with aberrant CD117 expression”, CD4+/CD8+ or CD4- /CD8-.

•B-cell markers-, CD13-, CD33-, and CD16-.

•Few cases are CD3-, CD7-, CD45-/partial+, CD11C+, CD25+, CD56+, or HLA-DR+.

Large Granular Lymphocyte Leukemia

•CD3+, CD2+, CD5-/dim/partial and/or CD7-/dim/partial

•CD4-/CD8+. Rare cases are CD4+/CD8+, CD4+/CD8- or CD4-/CD8-.

•TCRαβ+,

•CD11b, CD11c, CD57, CD16 and CD56 are variable, with no CD16/CD56 coexpression.

Chronic lymphoproliferative disorder of NK-cells (Large granular lymphocyte

leukemia with NK-cell Phenotype): CD3-, CD5-, CD2+, CD7+, CD4-/CD8- or CD4- CD8+, CD16+, CD56+ with CD16+/CD56+ coexpression and CD57+.

Original page 68

•TCRγδ large granular lymphocyte leukemia: sCD3+, CD2+, CD5+, CD7+, CD4- /CD8+ or CD4-/CD8-, CD11c+, CD16 variable, CD56 variable, and CD57 variable, with possible coexpression of CD56 and CD57 or CD16/CD57.

Adult T-Cell Leukemia/Lymphoma

•CD3+, CD2+, CD5+, CD7-, CD16-, CD56-, CD57-, TIA-1-, granzyme-, and TCRαβ+, or TCRαβ-/TCRγδ-.

•CD25+,CD11b-, and CD11c-.

•CD4+/CD8-. Rare cases are CD4-/CD8+ or CD4+/CD8+.

Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma

•High forward scatter, high side scatter,

•CD45+,

•CD3-, CD2+, CD7-, CD5-, TCRαβ+, CD4+/CD8-, and CD25+.

•CD30+ with strong membrane staining and perinuclear Golgi accentuation.

•CD43+, HLA-DR+, and EMA+.

•Nuclear/nucleolar, or cytoplasmic ALK+ in cases with t(2;5) and cytoplasmic ALK+ with other translocations.

•The ALK-negative variant: CD30 strong, and loss of most of pan-T markers.

Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome

–Mycosis Fungoides:

•CD45+

•CD3+, CD7-,

•TCRαβ+, and CD26 dim.

•Abnormal expression of pan-T markers (CD2-, CD3-, and/or CD5-),

Original page 69

•CD4+/CD8-. Rare cases are CD4-/CD8+.

–Sézary Syndrome: Diagnostic criteria include one or more of the following:

•Absolute Sézary cell count > 1000 cells/ mm. 3

•Immunophenotypical abnormalities (an expanded CD4+/CD8- T-cell population with a CD4/CD8 ratio > 10, loss of any or all of the pan-T cell markers or both).

•Peripheral blood T-cell clone by molecular or cytogenetic methods.
